block/recap: A residual block adds its input back: y equals x plus F of x. Its layers, F, only learn the change, what is left over: the residual.
block/conv: In a ConvNet, x is a stack of channels, and F is two convs with a ReLU between. Here F names the layers, not a filter size.
block/entries: The sum goes entry by entry, at every channel and position. Take three of x's numbers: two plus a half is two and a half, and so on down.
block/relu: In the first residual networks, from Kaiming He and colleagues in 2015, a ReLU follows the sum. So the minus a half becomes zero, while the two and a half and the two stay.
clash/stages: But a ConvNet changes shape as it goes: stage by stage, fewer positions and more channels. So some residual blocks have to change the shape themselves.
clash/x: Take an x with sixty four channels, eight by eight: sixty four by eight by eight.
clash/first: This block's first conv, with a hundred and twenty eight filters, makes a hundred and twenty eight channels. And its stride is two, so it lands on every other position.
clash/round: Its width: eight minus three, plus two for the padding, over two, plus one, is four and a half, rounded down to four.
clash/second: The second conv, stride one and padding one, keeps four by four. So F of x is a hundred and twenty eight by four by four.
clash/clash: Now try the sum. F of x is twice as deep as x, and half as wide. Their entries do not pair up one to one, so the two cannot be added.
fit/need: So the shortcut has to reshape x the same way, while changing as little else as it can. It gets a conv of its own, with filters one position wide: a one by one conv.
fit/mix: A one by one filter still reaches through every channel. At each position, it mixes the sixty four numbers there into one, and looks at nothing around them.
fit/filters: A hundred and twenty eight such filters make a hundred and twenty eight channels, as many as F makes.
fit/stride: Stride two, with no padding, lands on every other position, the very positions F's first conv was centered on. Eight minus one, over two, plus one, is four and a half: four.
fit/sum: So the shortcut gives a hundred and twenty eight by four by four, the shape of F of x, and the sum works.
fit/proj: The 2015 paper matched shapes this way in its deepest networks, and called it a projection shortcut: it carries x over into F's shape.
fit/same: In every block that keeps the shape, the shortcut stays x itself, with nothing to learn.
